questions.stem: A 50-year-old patient was diagnosed with pulmonary aspergillosis. The patient was a kidney transplant patient on the immunosuppressive regimen of tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone. Other medications included amlodipine. The patient was started on voriconazole 200 mg by mouth twice daily. One week later, the voriconazole trough serum concentration was 3.1 μg/mL, and the patient reported a “sunburn” despite being indoors most of the last week.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Change to anidulafungin 100 mg by mouth once daily
Change to fluconazole 400 mg by mouth once daily
Change to posaconazole DR tablets 300 mg once daily
Continue voriconazole 200 mg by mouth twice daily
Decrease voriconazole to 200 mg once daily

questions.explanation: Change to posaconazole DR tablets 300 mg once daily Voriconazole is the only azole known to carry the risk of photosensitivity reactions, including an association with skin cancers. Voriconazole is at steady state after 1 week of therapy, and the timing of the level (trough) is appropriate. The level is therapeutic (between 2 and 5.5 μg/mL). However, the adverse drug reaction is most likely attributed to voriconazole, and with other available treatment options, it would be best to use another agent. Continuing the voriconazole as is and decreasing the voriconazole are not the best options. Fluconazole does not have activity against Aspergillus. While echinocandins have activity against Aspergillus, anidulafungin monotherapy is inappropriate. Changing voriconazole to posaconazole is the most appropriate option.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q7

questions.stem: A 30-year-old patient was diagnosed with disseminated histoplasmosis. The patient was known to have HIV , well controlled on cobicistat/darunavir 150/800 mg and tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine 25/200 mg by mouth once daily. The patient did not take any other medications. Kidney and liver function were normal. The patient weighed 60 kg and had no known allergies.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate medication regimen for empiric maintenance therapy for disseminated histoplasmosis?

options.text: Itraconazole capsules 200 mg by mouth twice daily
Itraconazole capsules 400 mg by mouth once daily
Itraconazole oral solution 200 mg by mouth once daily
Itraconazole oral solution 200 mg by mouth twice daily
Liposomal amphotericin B 300 mg IV once daily

questions.explanation: Itraconazole oral solution 200 mg by mouth once daily Itraconazole is the recommended treatment of disseminated histoplasmosis during the maintenance phase of therapy. The itraconazole oral solution formulation is preferred over the capsule formulation due to increased bioavailability. Itraconazole doses greater than 200 mg should be split into multiple doses to help optimize absorption. Itraconazole is a major substrate of CYP450 3A4. Cobicistat/darunavir is a strong CYP450 3A4 inhibitor, which will decrease the metabolism of itraconazole, resulting in increased itraconazole levels. Itraconazole inhibits the metabolism of cobicistat/darunavir, resulting in an increase in darunavir. The interaction is clinically significant. The usual, i.e., in the setting of no drug–drug interactions, itraconazole maintenance dose is 200 mg by mouth twice daily. With these drug–drug interactions in place, the recommendation is to reduce the itraconazole dose to 200 mg once daily, and then check itraconazole levels.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q6

questions.question: Explain the resistance mechanism of Candida to fluconazole.
questions.question_raw: Explain the resistance mechanism of Candida to fluconazole

parts.text: Explain the resistance mechanism of Candida to fluconazole.

parts_raw.text: Explain the resistance mechanism of Candida to fluconazole

questions.model_answer: Candida resists fluconazole by several mechanisms, often in combination: (1) Overexpression/upregulation of ERG11 (the target, lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase), increasing enzyme levels so the drug cannot fully suppress ergosterol synthesis. (2) Point mutations in ERG11 altering the azole-binding site so fluconazole binds poorly. (3) Upregulation of efflux pumps — ATP-binding cassette transporters (CDR1/CDR2) and major facilitator superfamily pumps (MDR1) — that reduce intracellular drug concentration. (4) Bypass/loss-of-function mutations in ERG3, preventing accumulation of the toxic 14-alpha-methyl sterol that normally results from azole blockade.

questions.question: What are three indications for prophylaxis with posaconazole in clinical trials that have shown decreased mortality?
questions.question_raw: What are 3 indications for prophylaxis with Posaconazole in clinical trials that have shown decreased mortality?

parts.text: Three indications for posaconazole prophylaxis showing decreased mortality.

parts_raw.text: 3 indications for Posaconazole prophylaxis showing decreased mortality

questions.model_answer: (1) Prolonged neutropenia from remission-induction chemotherapy for newly diagnosed or first-relapse AML or MDS (Cornely, NEJM 2007 — reduced invasive fungal infections and lower all-cause mortality vs fluconazole/itraconazole). (2) Allogeneic HSCT recipients with GVHD on intensive immunosuppression (Ullmann, NEJM 2007 — reduced invasive aspergillosis and fewer fungal-related deaths vs fluconazole). (3) High-risk hematologic malignancy patients with anticipated protracted neutropenia (ANC <500 for ≥7 days), the population encompassed by these RCTs.
questions.beyond_mandell: Pivotal RCTs: Cornely NEJM 2007;356:348; Ullmann NEJM 2007;356:335.

cohort_answer.text: Prevention of invasive fungal infection, lower mortality in patients with prolonged neutropenia from AML; MDS; Prevention of death as antifungal prophylaxis for GVHD. 1. Posaconazole was superior to fluconazole or itraconazole in prevention of proven or probable invasive fungal infection and resulted in lower mortality from any cause and longer survival free from proven or probable invasive fungal infection (patients with or anticipated to have neutropenia, ANC <=500 cells/mm3 for >=7 days, from remission-induction chemotherapy for newly diagnosed or first relapse AML or MDS) - Cornely et al., NEJM 2007;356(4):348-359. 2. Posaconazole was similar to fluconazole for prophylaxis against fungal infections among patients with GVHD; superior in preventing invasive aspergillosis and reducing deaths related to fungal infections (patients with GVHD receiving immunosuppressive therapy) - Ullmann et al., NEJM 2007;356(4):335-347.

questions.question: For the following antibiotics, provide the mechanism of interaction with tacrolimus: ciprofloxacin, voriconazole, rifampin, clarithromycin.

parts.text: For the following antibiotics, provide the mechanism of interaction with tacrolimus: ciprofloxacin, voriconazole, rifampin, clarithromycin.

parts_raw.text: For the following antibiotics, provide the mechanism of interaction with tacrolimus: Cipro, Vori, Rifampin, Clarithromycin

questions.model_answer: Tacrolimus is a CYP3A4 substrate, so interactions reflect each drug's effect on CYP3A4. (1) Ciprofloxacin - weak/negligible CYP3A4 inhibition; little clinically significant effect on tacrolimus (monitor). (2) Voriconazole - potent CYP3A4 inhibitor; markedly increases tacrolimus levels (tacrolimus dose reduction required). (3) Rifampin - potent inducer of hepatic/intestinal CYP3A4, decreasing tacrolimus AUC/levels and risking acute graft rejection; rifabutin (least enzyme induction) is preferred in transplant recipients. (4) Clarithromycin - potent CYP3A4 inhibitor; increases tacrolimus levels.
questions.beyond_mandell: Ciprofloxacin, voriconazole and clarithromycin mechanisms are established pharmacology (Mandell rifamycin chapter covers only the rifampin/tacrolimus interaction and rifabutin as preferred alternative).

cohort_answer.text: Ciprofloxacin: no clear known interaction (immunologic effects postulated, unlikely clinically relevant). Voriconazole: likely inhibition of CYP3A4 leading to increased tacrolimus levels. Rifampin: suspected induction of CYP3A4 leading to decreased tacrolimus levels. Clarithromycin: strong CYP3A4 inhibition leading to increased tacrolimus levels.

questions.model_answer:
a) Caspofungin over fluconazole - azoles inhibit CYP3A4 and interact with carbamazepine (altered levels/toxicity), whereas the echinocandin has minimal CYP interaction.
b) Atovaquone over dapsone - dapsone causes oxidant hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
c) Doxycycline over clindamycin - clindamycin is strongly associated with C. difficile, while doxycycline is neither a C. difficile therapy nor a notable inducer of it. (Metronidazole is a C. difficile treatment, so it does not fit "not used for treatment.")
d) Levofloxacin over moxifloxacin - levofloxacin is renally excreted with high urinary concentrations, whereas moxifloxacin achieves poor urinary levels.
e) Valganciclovir over acyclovir - ganciclovir/valganciclovir is active against CMV; acyclovir is not reliably.
f) Ceftriaxone over cefuroxime - ceftriaxone reliably penetrates the CNS and is a standard meningitis agent, whereas cefuroxime has been associated with delayed CSF sterilization/meningitis failures.

questions.model_answer: a) Chronic kidney disease (CrCl 35 mL/min). The IV formulation is solubilized in the excipient sulfobutylether-beta-cyclodextrin (SBECD), which accumulates when CrCl is below 50 mL/min; the monograph therefore advises avoiding IV voriconazole (or using it cautiously) and preferring the oral formulation, which contains no cyclodextrin, once CrCl is <50 mL/min. b) Check a trough level after at least 5 days (steady state), i.e. the minimum is ~5 days of therapy (sooner only if a loading dose was given and early assessment is needed). c) Target trough: approximately 1–1.5 mg/L (≥ ~1–2 mg/L) for efficacy, and keep <5–6 mg/L to limit toxicity — i.e. a therapeutic window of roughly 1–5.5 mg/L.
questions.beyond_mandell: Cyclodextrin-accumulation caution and TDM targets are from the voriconazole product monograph and IDSA aspergillosis guidance.

parts_raw.text: Describe the interaction of tacrolimus (a CYP3A4 substrate) with each of the listed drugs.

questions.model_answer: (1) Ciprofloxacin - only weak CYP3A4 inhibition; minimal clinically important change in tacrolimus. (2) Voriconazole - potent CYP3A4 inhibitor; substantially increases tacrolimus levels, requiring dose reduction. (3) Rifampin - potent CYP3A4/intestinal enzyme inducer; decreases tacrolimus AUC and levels, risking subtherapeutic immunosuppression and acute graft rejection; rifabutin (least CYP3A4 induction) is the preferred rifamycin in transplant patients. (4) Clarithromycin - potent CYP3A4 inhibitor; increases tacrolimus levels.
questions.beyond_mandell: Ciprofloxacin, voriconazole and clarithromycin mechanisms are established pharmacology; the rifamycin chapter covers only the rifampin interaction and rifabutin as the preferred transplant alternative.

cohort_answer.text: Tacrolimus is a CYP3A4 substrate. Ciprofloxacin - weakly inhibits CYP3A4, may increase tacrolimus. Voriconazole - inhibits CYP3A4, increases tacrolimus. Rifampin - induces CYP3A4, decreases tacrolimus levels (strongest contraindication; rifabutin should be used instead of rifampin to avoid interaction and reduce risk of acute graft rejection). Clarithromycin (and other macrolides) - inhibits CYP3A4, increases tacrolimus.

b) (1) Gentamicin + tacrolimus - no true CYP-mediated interaction, but additive nephrotoxicity (both cause renal injury/acute kidney injury). (2) Mycophenolate mofetil + TMP-SMX - no true CYP interaction, but additive myelosuppression (leukopenia/cytopenias).

cohort_answer.text: Rifampin - induces CYP3A4, decreases tacrolimus. Clarithromycin - inhibits CYP3A4, increases tacrolimus. Fluconazole - inhibits CYP3A4, increases tacrolimus. Gentamicin + tacrolimus: no true drug-drug interaction, but both can cause nephrotoxicity. MMF + TMP/SMX: no true DDI, both can cause myelosuppression.

What are three common mechanisms of resistance?

parts_raw.text: What is their molecular target
What are three common mechanisms of resistance

questions.model_answer: a) Lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (CYP51/ERG11 gene product), the enzyme converting lanosterol to ergosterol; inhibition disrupts the fungal cell membrane. b) Any three of: (1) target-site mutation in ERG11/CYP51A reducing azole binding, (2) overexpression of efflux pumps (CDR/MDR genes), (3) overexpression of the target enzyme (ERG11 upregulation), (4) bypass/alteration of the sterol pathway (ERG3 mutation).

cohort_answer.text: Target: Inhibit lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, an enzyme necessary for conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol, a vital component of cellular membrane; disruptions cause significant membrane damage by increasing permeability, resulting in cell lysis and death. Resistance mechanisms: Upregulation of CDR and MDR genes (efflux pumps); Mutation in ERG11 gene (target site alteration, overexpression); Mutation of the ERG3 gene (bypass pathway); Alterations in the gene cyp51A

parts.text: What initial empiric antifungal therapy (from two different classes) would you use?
State three indications for urgent surgery present in this case.

parts_raw.text: What initial empiric antifungal therapy (from 2 different classes) would you use?
What are 3 indications for urgent surgery present in this case.
He is deemed not a candidate for valvular surgery. Based on the 2016 AHA/IDSA guidelines, what is the recommended antifungal management in this case?

questions.model_answer:
a) Initial empiric antifungal therapy combining two classes: (1) a polyene — lipid/liposomal amphotericin B (3-5 mg/kg/day), preferably with flucytosine (25 mg/kg/dose QID); PLUS (2) a high-dose echinocandin. Mandell notes amphotericin B plus 5-fluorocytosine and that echinocandins are encouraging for fungal IE.
b) Three indications for urgent surgery present here: (1) Fungal (Candida) endocarditis — infection that cannot be eradicated with antimicrobial therapy alone (ineffective antimicrobial therapy); (2) Severe aortic regurgitation with heart failure (hemodynamic compromise/CHF), the crucial determinant for valve replacement; (3) Large vegetation (13 mm) with systemic embolic phenomena (multiple splenic lesions).
c) When not a surgical candidate: complete the induction course with amphotericin B-based therapy and document clearance of candidemia, then step down (if the isolate is fluconazole-susceptible and the patient is stable) to oral fluconazole 400-800 mg (6-12 mg/kg) daily as long-term/lifelong chronic suppressive therapy because of the high risk of relapse.
questions.beyond_mandell: The specific step-down-to-fluconazole and lifelong suppression strategy is from the 2016 AHA IE scientific statement / IDSA Candida guidelines; Mandell confirms only long-term suppressive antifungal therapy in general.

cohort_answer.text: Empiric therapy: Liposomal amphoB (3-5mg/kg) +/- flucytosine; High dose echinocandin. Urgent surgery indications: Fungal endocarditis; Severe heart failure with valve dysfunction; Large mobile vegetation with evidence of embolic phenomena. If not a surgical candidate: Step down therapy to fluconazole 400-800mg daily if susceptible isolates, clinical stability, and cleared bloodstream Candida; for patients who cannot undergo valve replacement, long term suppression with fluconazole 400-800mg daily if isolate susceptible; even with surgery, reasonable to consider lifelong prophylaxis due to recurrence risk

parts_raw.text: For posaconazole prophylaxis, name three groups for which there is RCT data demonstrating decreased mortality and invasive fungal infections.

questions.model_answer: (1) Patients with prolonged neutropenia from remission-induction chemotherapy for AML or myelodysplastic syndrome (Cornely et al., NEJM 2007 — fewer invasive fungal infections and lower all-cause mortality vs fluconazole/itraconazole). (2) Allogeneic HSCT recipients with graft-versus-host disease receiving intensive immunosuppression (Ullmann et al., NEJM 2007 — fewer invasive aspergillosis cases and fewer fungal-related deaths vs fluconazole). (3) More broadly, high-risk hematologic malignancy patients with anticipated prolonged neutropenia, the populations in which these two RCTs established mortality benefit.
questions.beyond_mandell: Cornely NEJM 2007;356:348 and Ullmann NEJM 2007;356:335 are the pivotal RCTs.

questions.question: What is the molecular target of the following antifungals: posaconazole, micafungin, amphotericin, terbinafine?

parts.text: State the molecular target of each antifungal.

parts_raw.text: State the molecular target of each antifungal

questions.model_answer: Posaconazole: lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (Erg11/CYP51), blocking lanosterol-to-ergosterol conversion. Micafungin: 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase (inhibits fungal cell wall glucan synthesis). Amphotericin: ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane — polyene binds ergosterol and forms pores, increasing permeability. Terbinafine: squalene epoxidase, an early enzyme in the ergosterol biosynthesis pathway.

cohort_answer.text: Posaconazole - 14-alpha demethylase inhibitor (stops lanosterol to ergosterol). Micafungin - 1,3-beta-glucan synthetase enzyme inhibitor (fungal cell wall). Amphotericin - polyene, binds irreversibly to ergosterol in fungal cell membrane, increases permeability. Terbinafine - Squalene oxidase/epoxidase inhibitor (early step in ergosterol pathway).

questions.model_answer: Key distinguishing reasons for each pair: Valganciclovir over valacyclovir - CMV activity. Famciclovir over acyclovir - better oral bioavailability/less frequent dosing for HSV/VZV. Atovaquone over dapsone - G6PD deficiency (avoid dapsone hemolysis). Doxycycline over TMP-SMX - G6PD deficiency or need to avoid sulfa/renal dosing. Liposomal amphotericin B over amphotericin deoxycholate - less nephrotoxicity/infusion toxicity. Fluconazole over caspofungin - need CNS/urinary penetration or oral therapy (azole penetrates; echinocandins do not). Azithromycin over clarithromycin - fewer CYP3A4 drug interactions. Metronidazole over clindamycin - avoid C. difficile risk. Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin - better anaerobic/respiratory coverage (conversely levofloxacin for urinary/renal penetration). Piperacillin-tazobactam over meropenem - carbapenem-sparing to reduce resistance pressure when adequate. Ampicillin over cloxacillin - Enterococcus or Listeria coverage. Cefazolin over cloxacillin - convenient dosing/efficacy for MSSA (or penicillin allergy considerations).
